## Build the report

The report outline supplies headings; the table below supplies input identifiers. Write your own named chunks;
reuse the API and caching skills from the earlier bioinformatics modules.

| Gene | Ensembl ID |
|---|---|
| CDK1 | ENSG00000170312 |
| CDK4 | ENSG00000135446 |
| CDK6 | ENSG00000105810 |
| BCL2 | ENSG00000171791 |
| MCL1 | ENSG00000143384 |
| BCL2L1 | ENSG00000171552 |

## Query and flatten nested data

POST a JSON object with a `query` string to
`https://api.platform.opentargets.org/api/v4/graphql`. Use `httr2::request()`,
`req_body_json()` and `req_perform()`. Request one target at a time (six calls),
with this tested selection:

```graphql
query {
  target(ensemblId: "ENSG00000170312") {
    id
    approvedSymbol
    depMapEssentiality {
      tissueId
      tissueName
      screens { cellLineName geneEffect }
    }
  }
}
```

Also retrieve `{ meta { dataVersion { year month iteration } } }`. Check for a GraphQL `errors` member even
when HTTP status is 200. A changed schema is an error, not an empty biological result.

1. Read the JSON without automatic simplification (`simplifyVector = FALSE`) so
   the nested tissue and screen lists remain explicit.
2. Loop through each target, each tissue, and each screen. Produce one row per
   gene–cell-line result: `gene`, `ensembl_id`, `tissue_id`, `tissue`, `cell_line`, `gene_effect`.
3. Some tissue ontology IDs are null (the `other` group has no ID). Preserve the tissue name and use an empty ID string; a null identifier must not discard a valid screen. Remove only rows whose gene-effect value is missing; keep zero and positive values.
4. Cache the flattened data and release metadata. With `use_snapshot <- TRUE`,
   read the shipped files. Record the **snapshot retrieval date**, not today's date,
   when using those files.

## Plot distributions

Make a violin plot of `gene_effect` by `gene`, then show BCL2 values by tissue.
Add a horizontal reference at −1 and label it as a normalisation reference, not a
universal cutoff. Display sample sizes; very small tissue groups do not support
strong comparisons. A dot plot or boxplot can complement violins when groups are small.

## Tasks

**T4.** Which tissues contain BCL2-sensitive cell lines? Is the median alone enough? `[ELO 8, 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-18)"}
Blood/haematopoietic and lymphoid groups contain sensitive lines, consistent with the rationale for BCL2 inhibition in some blood cancers. Yet most lines in the full dataset have BCL2 effects near zero, and other groups also contain sensitive lines. Plot the lower tail and sample sizes; do not claim all blood cancers are BCL2 dependent or infer a unique tissue specificity from a median.
:::

**T5. [VG]** A cell line is strongly MCL1 dependent and weakly BCL2 dependent. Does this prove venetoclax will kill it? `[ELO 8, 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-18)"}
No. Venetoclax targets BCL2, while this screen suggests reliance on a different anti-apoptotic protein, MCL1. Test drug dose–response and apoptosis, verify target engagement, and compare genetic perturbations. Compensation and the difference between knockout and inhibition can change the result.
:::

**T6.** What three limitations belong below your plot? `[ELO 7, 8, 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-18)"}
For example: cultured cell lines are selected models of tumours; gene effect depends on the assay/release and growth conditions; knockout differs from a drug; tissue groups are unbalanced; dependency is not expression. Include the limitations that affect your actual comparison.
:::

## Hand-in (optional)

One HTML report: question, source/release/retrieval date, reproducible code, two
labelled plots, interpretation with uncertainty, and `sessionInfo()`. Include at
least one inline number calculated from your data. State whether you used live data
or the dated snapshot.
